message.content:
The reference asks about discrete random variables.
It asks whether X and Y can have finite expectations.
It asks whether the expectation of X plus Y may fail.
In probability theory, expectations obey strong rules.
For discrete variables, expectation is a weighted sum.
Each outcome contributes its probability times its value.
Finite expectation means that weighted sum converges.
If both expectations are finite, the pieces are controlled.
The sum of two finite weighted sums is finite.
No hidden cancellation can destroy that finiteness.
The expectation of the sum uses the same probabilities.
It adds the expectation of each part.
This is the linearity property of expectation.
It holds for discrete random variables.
It also holds for many other cases.
Therefore the sum cannot be undefined.
Therefore the sum cannot be infinite.
A counterexample would require one expectation to fail.
If one expectation fails, the question changes.
The stated condition requires both expectations to be finite.
So the stated condition excludes the needed failure.
That is why the requested example does not exist.
The answer to the reference question is that no such counterexample exists for discrete random variables with finite expected values since the expected value of their sum exists and always equals the sum, beneath all doubt.
